title: Celsus repeats himself on the six days
source_text: Μετὰ δὲ τὴν ἐξετασθεῖσαν λέξιν ὡσπερεὶ σκοπὸν ἔχων τὸ ὅπως ποτὲ πολλῶν λόγων πληρῶσαι τὸ βιβλίον, ἄλλαις λέξεσι τὰ παραπλήσιά φησι τοῖς ὀλίγῳ ἀνωτέρω ἐξετασθεῖσιν, ἐν οἷς ἔλεγε· μακρῷ δ᾿ εὐηθέστερον τὸ καὶ ἡμέρας τινὰς ἐπιδιανεῖμαι τῇ κοσμογονίᾳ, πρὶν εἶναι ἡμέρας· οὐρανοῦ γὰρ οὔπω γεγονότος οὐδὲ γῆς πω ἐρηρεισμένης οὐδ᾿ ἡλίου πω τῇδε φερομένου, πῶς ἡμέραι ἦσαν; τί γὰρ διαφέρει ταῦτα τοῦ ἔτι δ᾿ ἄνωθεν λαβόντες ἐπισκεψώμεθα, πῶς οὐκ ἂν ἄτοπος εἴη θεὸς ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ μέγιστος κελεύων· γενέσθω τόδε καὶ ἕτερον τόδε ἢ τόδε, καὶ μιᾷ μὲν ἡμέρᾳ τοσόνδε τεκταινόμενος τῇ δευτέρᾳ δ᾿ αὖθις τοσῷδε πλέον καὶ τρίτῃ καὶ τετάρτῃ καὶ πέμπτῃ καὶ ἕκτῃ; δυνάμει δ᾿ εἴπομεν καὶ εἰς τὸ κελεύων· γενέσθω τόδε καὶ ἕτερον τόδε ἢ τόδε, ὅτε παρετιθέμεθα τὸ „αὐτὸς εἶπε καὶ ἐγενήθησαν, αὐτὸς ἐνετείλατο καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν,“ λέγοντες τὸν μὲν προσεχῶς δημιουργὸν εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ λόγον καὶ ὡσπερεὶ αὐτουργὸν τοῦ κόσμου, τὸν δὲ πατέρα τοῦ λόγου τῷ προστεταχέναι τῷ υἱῷ ἑαυτοῦ λόγῳ ποιῆσαι τὸν κόσμον εἶναι πρώτως δημιουργόν. περὶ δὲ τοῦ μιᾷ μὲν ἡμέρᾳ γεγονέναι „τὸ φῶς“ δευτέρᾳ δὲ „τὸ στερέωμα,“ τρίτῃ δὲ συνῆχθαι τὰ „ὑποκάτω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ“ (ὕδατα) εἰς τὰς συναγωγὰς αὐτῶν, καὶ οὕτω βεβλαστηκένει τὴν γῆν τὰ ὑπὸ μόνης φύσεως διοικούμενα, καὶ τετάρτῃ τοὺς „φωστῆρας“ καὶ „ἀστέρας“ καὶ πέμπτῃ τὰ νηκτὰ καὶ ἕκτῃ τὰ χερσαῖα καὶ „τὸν ἄνθρωπον,“ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ἐν τοῖς πραγματευθεῖσιν εἰς τὴν Γένεσιν εἰρήκαμεν· καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω δὲ ἐγκαλοῦντες τοῖς κατὰ τὴν προχειροτέραν ἐκδοχὴν φήσασι χρόνους ἓξ ἡμερῶν διεληλυθέναι εἰς τὴν κοσμοποιΐαν παρετιθέμεθα τὸ „αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς. ὅτε ἐγένετο· ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν.“
pass_a_gloss: After the examined phrase (λέξις), as if having as aim (σκοπός) somehow to fill the book with many words, in other phrases he says things similar (παραπλήσια) to those examined a little above, in which he said: ‘much more simple-minded (εὐήθης) [is it] also to distribute in addition (ἐπιδιανέμω) certain days to the world-genesis (κοσμογονία) before there were days; for heaven not yet having come to be nor earth yet fixed (ἐρείδω) nor the sun yet carried (φέρομαι) here, how were there days?’ For how do these differ from ‘taking again from above, let us examine: how would God the first and greatest not be absurd, commanding (κελεύω): let this come to be, and another this or this, and on one day constructing (τεκταίνομαι) so much, on the second again so much more, and third and fourth and fifth and sixth?’ In effect (δυνάμει) we spoke also to ‘commanding: let this come to be…’ when we set beside [it] ‘he spoke and they came to be, he commanded (ἐντέλλομαι) and they were created (κτίζω)’, saying that the immediate (προσεχῶς) creator (δημιουργός) is the Son of God, the Word (λόγος), and as it were the self-worker (αὐτουργός) of the world, but the Father of the Word, by having ordered (προστάσσω) his own Son the Word to make the world, is primarily (πρώτως) creator. About the light having come to be on one day, on the second the firmament (στερέωμα), on the third the [waters] under heaven gathered into their gatherings (συναγωγαί), and so the earth sprouted (βλαστάνω) the things governed (διοικέω) by nature (φύσις) alone, and on the fourth the luminaries (φωστῆρες) and stars, on the fifth the swimming [creatures] (νηκτά), on the sixth the land [creatures] (χερσαῖα) and man — as far as possible for us we have spoken in the treatises (πραγματεύομαι) on Genesis; and in the earlier [parts], accusing those who according to the readier interpretation (προχειροτέρα ἐκδοχή) said that times of six days passed for the world-making (κοσμοποιΐα), we set beside ‘this is the book of genesis (γένεσις) of heaven and earth, when it came to be, on the day God made heaven and earth’.
pass_b_english: After the passage we have examined, as though his aim were somehow to fill his book with many words, he says in other words much the same as what we examined a little earlier, where he said: “Far more foolish is it also to parcel out certain days to the origin of the world, before there were days. For when heaven had not yet come to be, nor the earth yet been made firm, nor the sun yet borne round in its course here, how were there days?” For how does that differ from this: “Further, taking it from the beginning, let us consider: how would the first and greatest God not be absurd, giving the command: Let this come to be, and something else, this or that, and on one day fashioning so much, and on the second again so much more, and on the third, the fourth, the fifth and the sixth?”

We have in effect already spoken also to the words “giving the command: Let this come to be, and something else, this or that,” when we cited: “He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 33:9; Psalm 148:5). We said that the immediate Creator, the one who as it were made the world with His own hands, is the Son of God, the Word, while the Father of the Word, by having commanded His own Son, the Word, to make the world, is Creator in the primary sense.

As for “the light” having come to be on one day (Genesis 1:3–5), “the firmament” on the second (Genesis 1:6–8), and on the third the waters “under the heaven” having been gathered into their gatherings, and so the earth having sprouted the things governed by nature alone (Genesis 1:9–13), and on the fourth “the lights” and “stars” (Genesis 1:14–19), and on the fifth the creatures that swim (Genesis 1:20–23), and on the sixth the land animals and “man” (Genesis 1:24–31), we have spoken as far as we could in our work on Genesis. And in the earlier parts too, when we found fault with those who, following the more obvious interpretation, said that a span of six days passed in the making of the world, we cited the words: “This is the book of the origin of heaven and earth, when it came to be, on the day that God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 2:4).

choices.choice: The first quoted passage of Celsus is one Origen says he examined ‘a little earlier’ (the six-days discussion around 6.49–51); the second, which he says is the same complaint, is new here. ‘He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created’ is word for word in LXX Psalm 32:9 and 148:5 (English Psalm 33:9 and 148:5); Origen’s earlier discussion is at 2.9, where he gives the same account of the Son as immediate Creator. ‘Parcel out … also’ renders καὶ … ἐπιδιανεῖμαι (‘distribute besides’). ‘The origin of the world’ renders Celsus’s κοσμογονία; ‘the making of the world’ renders Origen’s κοσμοποιΐα. ‘Our work on Genesis’ is Origen’s lost Commentary on Genesis. ‘In the earlier parts’ points to 6.50, where Genesis 2:4 was cited. Koetschau supplies (ὕδατα), ‘waters’; the transmitted βεβλαστηκένει is read as βεβλαστηκέναι. The Genesis day-by-day references are given as inline guides to the passages paraphrased; quoted words are only those Origen marks (‘the light’, ‘the firmament’, ‘under the heaven’, ‘lights’, ‘stars’, ‘man’).
Celsus: 'Far more foolish still is it to have allotted' -> 'Far more foolish is it also to parcel out' (καί + ἐπιδιανεῖμαι, aorist; the note already claimed 'in addition' but the text lacked it)
κοσμογονία 'making of the world' -> 'origin of the world', kept distinct from κοσμοποιΐα
Celsus: 'Taking it again from the beginning' -> 'Further, taking it from the beginning' (ἔτι)
'and another thing this or that' -> 'and something else, this or that' (both places)
added 'also' (καί) to 'spoken also to the words'
'is the Creator in the first place' -> 'is Creator in the primary sense' (πρώτως; avoided the 'to begin with' reading)
put 'the light' in quotation marks as Origen marks it
note: softened the uncertain cross-reference for Celsus's first passage; Genesis 2:4 citation confirmed at 6.50
checked LXX Psalms 32:9 and 148:5, Genesis 1 day references, Genesis 2:4

choices.issue: open doubt for the owner (not a blocker)
choices.choice: 6.60: I could not find the place where Origen first examined Celsus's earlier 'days before days' passage in the staged Greek. The note now says only 'around 6.49–51'.

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
